(Makkiyya/Madaniyya: [Madaniyya, and it is said] it is disputed; it has forty-three verses; [it was revealed after Surat Muhammad])

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

تِلْكَ (Tilka, "those") is a reference to the verses of the surah. By "the Book" is meant the surah, i.e., "those verses" are the verses of the complete surah, wondrous in its kind. Then he said: وَالَّذِي أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ ﴿And that which has been revealed to you﴾, from the Qur'an as a whole, "is the Truth" ﴿الْحَقُّ﴾, which admits of nothing further, not this surah alone. In the style of this statement is the saying of the woman of the Anmar tribe (al-Anmariyya): "They are like a ring (al-halqa) that is woven without end; one does not know where its two ends are." She means the perfection (al-kamla).

[Note: the gloss of the Anmariyya's words is "i.e., regarding her children." (Ē)]

Allah is the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" (the One who) is its predicate (khabar), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾. It is also permissible for "alladhi" to be an attribute (sifah). His saying "yudabbiru al-amr, yufassilu al-ayat" (He manages the affair, He details the signs) is a predicate after a predicate. What supports this is what precedes it, the mention of the signs. ﴿He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf), offered as evidence by their seeing them as such. It has also been said that "tarawnaha" is an attribute of "ʿamad" (pillars). This is strengthened by the reading of Ubayy: "tarawnahu" (you see it). It was also read "ʿumud" with two dammas. ﴿He manages the affair﴾: He manages the affair of His dominion (malakut) and lordship (rububiyyah). ﴿He details the signs﴾: He details His signs in His revealed books. ﴿So that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾: certain of the recompense (al-jaza', the reward), and certain that this One who manages and details is one to whom you must necessarily return. Al-Hasan read "nudabbiru" with a nun. ﴿And He made in it two mates, two﴾: He created in it, from all kinds of fruits, pairs, two by two, when He spread it out; then they multiplied afterwards and became diverse. It was also said: by "the two mates" is meant the black and the white, the sweet and the sour, the small and the large, and what resembles these of the various kinds. ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾: He dresses it in its place, so that it becomes black and dark after it had been white and bright. It was also read "yughshi" with the doubled ghayn (tashdid).

Pieces of land, adjacent to one another, in different soils: good land next to salty land, fertile land next to barren land, hard land next to soft land, and land suitable for crops but not for trees next to other land that is the reverse of it, yet all of them are united in the genus of earth. That is evidence of a capable and willing Creator, who arranges His acts in one way rather than another.[[On his words "zuhayda" (barren) in al-Sihah: a valley is zuhayd when it holds little water, and arḍ zihad (barren land) is land that floods only with heavy rain. (ʿ)]]

Likewise the crops, vineyards and palm trees that grow in these pieces are different in kind and type, and they are watered with one water, yet you see their fruits differing in shape, colour, taste and smell, and some excelling others in these qualities.

In some copies of the Qur'an the reading is "qiṭaʿan mutajāwirāt" (pieces, adjacent ones), with "wa-jaʿala" (and He made). It is also read "wa-jannāt" (and gardens) in the accusative, as a conjunction with "zawjayn" (two kinds), or in the genitive, as a conjunction with "al-thamarāt kulliha" (all the fruits). It is also read "wa-zarʿ wa-nakhīl" (and crops and palm trees) in the genitive, as a conjunction with "aʿnāb" (vineyards) or "jannāt" (gardens).

Al-ṣinwān (the clustered palms), the plural of ṣinw, is a palm tree that has two heads but one root. The word is read with a kasra on the initial sound and also with a ḍamma. The kasra is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, and the ḍamma is the dialect of Banū Tamīm and Qays.

"Yusqā" (is watered) is read with the letter tāʾ and with yāʾ. "Nufaḍḍil" (We favour) is read with nūn, and with yāʾ in the form that serves both the active and the passive as the verb (of the subject and the object). "Fī al-ukul" (in the food/fruit) is read with the kāf vowelled with a ḍamma or left with a sukūn.

And if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their saying in denial of the Resurrection, then their saying is indeed amazing and deserves to be wondered at. For whoever was able to create the great heavens that have been enumerated to you, and was not wearied by creating them, then restoring creation is the easiest and simplest thing for Him. So their denial is one of the marvels of marvels. ﴿When we have become dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ This may be in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for their saying, and it may be in the accusative, governed by the verb "say" (al-qawl), or governed by what is indicated by His saying ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾.

﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord﴾: those are the perfect ones who persist in their disbelief. ﴿And those, the shackles are on their necks﴾: this describes them as obstinate, like His saying ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles on their necks﴾. And similar to it is the verse:

They are lost, and the path of error is their destination...
For them, away from right guidance, are shackles and fetters.

"The path of error" is a figurative expression (majaz, figurative usage) for the wicked states they are in. The "ghull" (shackle) is that with which the hand is bound to the neck, and the "qayd" (fetter) is for the legs. Both are figurative for heedlessness and following the opinion of the self. He says: they took the path of desire and abandoned the path of guidance.

Or it is part of the threat (wa'id).

﴿Yastaʿjilūnaka bil-sayyiʾati qabla al-ḥasanah﴾ ("They ask you to hasten the evil before the good"): with punishment before well-being, and kindness toward them by granting respite. This is because they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to bring them the punishment, mocking his warning. ﴿Wa-qad khalat min qablihimu al-mathulāt﴾ ("And examples of punishment have already passed before them"): that is, the punishments inflicted on people like them among the deniers. So why do they not take heed from them and stop mocking?

Al-mathulah (exemplary punishment) means a punishment, on the pattern of al-samrah. It is called mathulah because of the correspondence (al-mumathalah) between the punishment and the one punished. ﴿Wa-jazāʾu sayyiʾatin sayyiʾatun mithluhā﴾ ("And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it"). It is said: amthaltu al-rajul min ṣāḥibih wa-aqwaṣtu minh (I took retribution from him on behalf of his companion, and exacted retaliation from him). Al-mithāl means retaliation (al-qiṣāṣ).

The reading al-mathulāt is also recited with two damma, the fāʾ making the ʿayn take a damma (li-ittibāʿ al-fāʾ al-ʿayn). Al-mathalāt, with a fatḥa on the mīm and sukūn on the thāʾ, is as in the saying "al-samrah". Al-muthulāt, with a ḍamma on the mīm and sukūn on the thāʾ, is a lightened form of al-mathulāt with two ḍammas. Al-mathulāt is the plural of mathulah, like rukbah and rukabāt (the knee; the plural of paucity is rukabāt, rukbāt, and rukubāt; in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, the knee is well known, and in its margin, from Murtaḍā: that is, with the kāf sukūn, ḍamma, or fatḥa, and the rāʾ is ḍammed in all of them).

﴿Inna rabbaka la-dhū maghfiratin lil-nās ʿalā ẓulmihim﴾ ("Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing"): that is, despite their wronging themselves through sins. ʿAla here is in the position of a circumstantial clause (al-ḥāl), meaning "while they are wrongdoers toward themselves".

[Editor's note: Al-Zamakhshari says: "ʿAla ẓulmihim is in the position of the circumstantial clause, meaning wronging themselves..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: The correct view is that the promise remains on its general application, except where evidence restricts it in cases other than the one who affirms divine unity (muwaḥḥid). For his wrongdoing, meaning his shirk, is not forgiven, while forgiveness of anything other than shirk is subject to God's will. Al-Zamakhshari builds on his doctrine, whose falsity has been made clear, regarding the impossibility of forgiveness for the perpetrator of major sins even if he is a muwaḥḥid, unless he repents. So he restricts it absolutely and narrows what is broad. And God is the Granter of success.]

There are several interpretations of this. One is that it means the minor sins (al-sayyiʾāt) that are expiated for one who avoids the major sins. Another is that it means the major sins, on condition of repentance. Another is that by forgiveness is meant concealment and respite.

It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for God's pardon and His overlooking, no one would have enjoyed life; and were it not for His threat and His punishment, every person would have relied entirely (on his deeds)."

[Editor's note: Ibn Abi Ḥātim and al-Thaʿlabī transmitted it from the narration of Ḥammād ibn Salamah from ʿAlī ibn Zayd from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab: "When the verse ﴿Wa-inna rabbaka la-dhū maghfirah﴾ (And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness) was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said..." and he mentioned it.]

﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ They did not accept the signs revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), out of obstinacy, and so they proposed signs like those of Musa and ʿIsa, such as the staff turning into a serpent and the raising of the dead. It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You are only a man sent as a warner, frightening them of the evil consequence, and an advisor like the other messengers. Your duty is only to bring that by which the truth of your being a warning messenger is established. That truth is established by any sign whatsoever. All signs are equal in establishing the validity of the call; there is no difference between them." He in whose knowledge is everything in due measure gives each prophet a sign according to what His knowledge of the interests requires and His determination of them. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾: a prophet who guides them to the religion and calls them to Allah by a way of guidance, and with a sign specific to him. He did not make the prophets one law [[His saying "and He did not make the prophets one law" means equal, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] with uniform signs.

Another interpretation: the meaning is that they deny that what was sent down to you consists of signs, and they are obstinate. So do not be concerned by that; you are only a warner. Your duty is only to warn, not to establish faith in their hearts, which you are not able to do. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾, able to guide them by compulsion, and that is Allah the Exalted.

By what follows, the mention of the signs of His knowledge and His determination of things, He has shown that His giving each warner signs different from those of another is a matter arranged by all-encompassing knowledge and measured by divine wisdom. Had He known that granting their proposal would bring good and benefit, He would have granted it to them. As for the second interpretation, it shows that the one whose power and knowledge are such is alone able to guide them, knowing by which path to guide them, and no one else has a way to that.

Allah knows what every female bears, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. Everything with Him is in measure. (Qur'an 13:8)

[The commentary begins here.]

**Allah knows** (ﷻ) ("Allahu ya'lamu") may be a new, independent sentence, or the meaning may be: "He is Allah," as an explanation of *hadha* in the last reading. Then it continues: **"He knows what every female bears."**

**"Ma"** in *ma tahmilu* and *ma taghidu* and *ma tazdadu* is either a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*, "that which") or a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*, "the fact that").

If it is a relative pronoun, the meaning is: He knows what she carries of offspring, whether it is male or female, complete or deficient (*khadaj*), beautiful or ugly, tall or short, and other conditions present and future. **"And He knows what the wombs diminish"**, that is, what they reduce. It is said: *ghada al-ma'u* and *ghadatuhu ana* (the water receded, and I made it recede). From this is the Qur'anic verse: ﴿and the water was made to subside﴾. **"And what they increase"**, that is, what they take in excess. You say: *akhadhtu minhu haqqi* (I took my right from him) and *izdadtu minhu kadha* (I took more from him than that). From this is the Qur'anic verse: ﴿and they added nine﴾. It is also said: *zadtuhu fazad bi-nafsihi wa-izdad* (I increased it, and it increased by itself).

What the womb diminishes and increases includes the number of offspring: it may contain one, and it may contain two, three, or four. It is related that Shurayk was the fourth of four in his mother's womb. Also included is the body of the child, which may be complete or deficient. Also included is the period of gestation, which may be less than nine months and may extend beyond that: up to two years according to Abu Hanifa, up to four according to al-Shafi'i, and up to five according to Malik. It is said that al-Dahhak was born after two years, and Harim ibn Hayyan remained in his mother's womb for four years, which is why he was named *Haram*. Also included is the blood, which may decrease or increase.

If *ma* is a verbal-noun particle, the meaning is that He knows the bearing of every female and knows the diminishing and increasing of the wombs; nothing of that is hidden from Him, nor its times and conditions.

It is also permissible that what is intended is the diminishing and increasing of what is in the wombs, and the verb is ascribed to the wombs while it really belongs to what is in them, on the basis that both verbs are intransitive. This is supported by the statement of al-Hasan: "*al-Ghaydhuda* is that she gives birth at eight months or less, and *al-izdiyad* is that she carries beyond nine months." Also from him: "*al-Ghayd* is what becomes a miscarriage before completion, and *al-izdiyad* is what is born at full term."

**"By measure"** (*bi-miqdar*): by a determined amount that it does not exceed and does not fall short of, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾.

**"Al-Kabir"** (the Great): the one of great dignity, before whom everything is lesser. **"Al-Muta'al"** (the Exalted): the one who is elevated above everything by His power, or the one who is far above the attributes of created beings and exalted beyond them.

**Sārib** means one who goes on his way (dhāhib fī sarbihi), with the vowel of the ra' pronounced as a fatha, that is, in his path and direction. It is said: *sarab fi'l-arḍ, surūban* (he went off into the land). The meaning is: "the same to Him is whoever hides himself," that is, seeks concealment in a hiding place by night, in its darkness, "and whoever moves about openly in the roads by day, so that everyone sees him." If you say: the proper wording should have been "and whoever is hiding by night and whoever is moving about by day," [[Mahmud said: "If you say the wording should have been: 'and whoever is hiding by night and whoever is moving about by day ...' etc." Ahmad said: The implication of the question raised by al-Zamakhshari is that the waw is conjunctive, joining one of the two attributes to the other, while the implication of his answer is that one of the two subjects is joined to the other. The verse admits another possibility: that the relative pronoun is elided and its relative clause remains. The meaning is: "and whoever is hiding by night and whoever is moving about by day." Eliding the relative pronoun of the conjoined item while its relative clause remains is common, especially since the relative pronoun has been repeated three times in the verse. An example is His saying, ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [46:9], the original being "nor what will be done with you," otherwise the negative particle would be misplaced, because if the second clause were taken as part of the first clause's relative clause through the conjunction, there would be no place for the negation. In the first case, the relative pronoun accompanies the clause, not the relative clause. Another example is the verse:

"Whoever among you mocks the Messenger of Allah,
and praises him and supports him, is one and the same."

That is: "and whoever praises him and supports him." And Allah knows best.]] so that the phrase covers the sense of equality between the one who hides and the one who moves about, otherwise it covers only one person who is both hiding and moving about. I say: there are two possibilities. The first is that His saying *wa-sārib* (and one who moves about) is conjoined to *man huwa mustakhfin* (whoever is hiding), not to *mustakhfin* (the hider) alone. The second is that it is conjoined to *mustakhfin*, but *man* carries the sense of the dual, as in the lines:

"Let us be like the one who, O wolf, goes along with us."

[[I spent the night dividing the provisions between him and me,
by the light of a fire at one time, and by its smoke at another.
When he bared his fangs as if laughing, and the hilt of my sword
was in my hand at a great distance from it, I said to him:
'Come, if you pledge yourself to me and promise not to betray me,
we shall be like the ones who, O wolf, keep company.'
'Are you a man, O wolf, when treachery and deceit are in you,
as though you were two brothers suckled on the same milk?'

By al-Farazdaq, describing a wolf that came to him in a desert, so he spent the night dividing the provisions between himself and it, while they were both sitting by the light of a fire at one time and by its smoke at another, indicating that it was repeatedly kindled. *Takashshara*: he bared his teeth as one laughing. *Qā'im sayfī*: that is, while the hilt of my sword was at a great distance from my hand, indicating eagerness and boldness. *Ta'āl*: come, that is, approach, so that we may make a pledge. It is also narrated as *ta'ash*, that is, eat supper. *Fa-in 'āhattanī*: if you make a covenant with me afterward and bind yourself not to betray me. *Nakun mithla man yā dhi'b yaṣṭaḥibān*: "we shall be like the ones who, O wolf, keep company." The word *man* is dual in meaning, so the resumptive pronoun returns to it accordingly. The vocative is a parenthetical insertion between the relative clause and the relative pronoun. *A-anta*: an interrogative of rebuke. Repeating the vocative also carries a kind of rebuke. *Akhyayn*: the diminutive of *akhawayn* (two brothers). *Al-labān*: specifically the milk of a woman. He likened the wolf and treachery to twin brothers raised together from infancy, suckled by a single mother, indicating complete inseparability and affinity. Calling the wolf "man" is based on treating it as if it were a rational being, which makes addressing it correct. He likened the two to brothers of the human kind, as the word *labān* indicates, because affinity in it is more complete and more evident than in other things.]]

as if it were said: "Two of you are equal: one hiding by night and one moving about by day." The pronoun in *lahu* (for him) refers back to *man* (whoever), as if it were said: "for whoever keeps secret and whoever speaks aloud, and whoever hides himself and whoever moves about openly, there are *mu'aqqibāt* (successive angels)," that is, groups of angels who follow one another in guarding and protecting him. The original form is *mu'taqibāt* (following one another), and the *tā'* was assimilated into the *qāf*, as in His saying ﴿And those who make excuses came﴾ [9:90], meaning *al-mu'tadhirūn* (those who make excuses). It is also permissible to read *mu'aqqibāt* with a kasra on the ayn, though it has not been recited that way. Or it is a form of *mufa''alāt* from *'aqabahu*, when one comes after him, as one says *qafā'* (the back of the head), because some of them follow others. Or because they follow up what is said and write it down. ﴿They guard him by the command of Allah﴾. Both are attributes, [[He returned to his speech. He said: The meaning of His saying ﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah﴾ is that both are attributes, and "by the command of Allah" is not a complement of the verb "guard." It is as if it were said: "For him are successive angels by the command of Allah." Ahmad said: The real sense of this view is that they guard him from the matter which Allah knows He will avert from him because of their supplication. Without this cause, it would be in Allah's knowledge that vengeance would fall upon him, because Allah, mighty and majestic, knows what would not occur, were it to occur, how it would occur. "Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge."]] and "by the command of Allah" is not a complement of the guarding; it is as if it were said: "For him are successive angels by the command of Allah." Or they guard him for the sake of the command of Allah, that is, for the sake of the fact that Allah commanded them to guard him. The evidence for this is the reading of ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn ʿAbbās, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, and ʿIkrimah: *yaḥfaẓūnahu bi-amr Allāh* (they guard him by the command of Allah). Or they guard him from the affliction and punishment of Allah if he sins, through their supplication for him and their request to their Lord that He grant him respite in hope that he will repent and turn back, like His saying ﴿Say: Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?﴾ [21:42]. It has also been said: *al-mu'aqqibāt* are the guards and the police (*al-jalāwizah*) around the ruler, who guard him in his imagination and estimation from the command of Allah, that is, from His decrees and calamities, or this is said in mockery of him. It is also read as *la-hu maʿāqīb*, the plural of *muʿaqqib* or *muʿaqqibah*.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 13, verse 14:**

The phrase ﴿the call of the truth﴾ has two possible meanings. The first is that the call is attributed to the truth, which is the opposite of falsehood, just as the word is attributed to it in your saying "the word of truth," to indicate that the call is connected with the truth, specific to it, and far removed from falsehood. The meaning is that God, glorified is He, is called upon and responds to the call, granting the caller his request if it is in his interest. So it is a call connected with the truth, because it is fitting that supplication be directed to Him, given the benefit and gain in answering it, unlike the supplication of one whose call brings no benefit and no good. The second meaning is that the call is attributed to the Truth, who is God, mighty and exalted, in the sense of: the call to the true One who hears and answers.

It is related from al-Hasan: "The Truth is God, and every call to Him is the call of the truth."

If you ask: how do these two descriptions connect with what precedes them? I answer: according to the story of Arbad, it is clear, because his being struck by the thunderbolt is a plot from God against him, coming upon him from where he did not perceive it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had prayed against him and his companion, saying: "O God, cause them to sink into the earth by whatever means You will," and they were answered in this matter, so the call was a call of truth.[1] As for the first interpretation, it is a threat to the disbelievers for their disputation with the Messenger of God, by making his plot descend upon them, and it is the answering of the call of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he prayed against them concerning them. ﴿And those they call upon besides God﴾, that is, the idols that the disbelievers call upon besides God, ﴿do not respond to them with anything﴾ of their requests, ﴿except like one who stretches out his hands toward water﴾, that is, except with a response like the response of one who stretches his palms out to water, asking it to reach his mouth. Water is inanimate; it does not perceive the stretching out of his palms, nor his thirst and need for it, and it cannot answer his plea and reach his mouth. Likewise, what they call upon is inanimate: it does not sense their calling, cannot respond to them, and cannot benefit them. It has been said: they are compared, in the futility of their supplication to their gods, to one who wants to scoop water with his hands to drink, so he spreads them out with his fingers extended, but his palms gather nothing of it and he does not attain his desire of drinking.

It is recited ﴿tad'un﴾ (you call) with the letter tā' (ta). And ﴿kabāsiṭi kaffayh﴾ with tanwīn (kabāsiṭun kaffayhi).[2] ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, that is, only in loss with no benefit in it, because if they call upon God He does not answer them, and if they call upon the idols, they cannot respond to them.

And to Allah prostrate (yasjudu) — that is, they submit to the bringing about of whatever He wills concerning them of His acts, whether they wish or refuse. They are not able to avoid Him, and their shadows too submit to Him, as they turn about according to His will in lengthening and shortening, in the shade and its receding. And it is recited: "bil-ghuduww wal-iṣāl" (in the mornings and the evenings), from āṣalū, meaning they entered the late afternoon (al-aṣīl).

Say, "Allah." This is a recounting of their acknowledgment and a confirmation against them, for when he says to them, "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?", they have no choice but to say, "Allah." Like His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne? They will say: Allah.﴾ This is like when a debater says to his opponent, "Is this your statement?" and when he says, "This is my statement," he says, "This is your statement," so his acknowledgment is recounted as a confirmation against him and as a securing of it from him. Then he says to him: "It will follow for you from this statement that such-and-such." It is also permissible that this is a prompting, meaning: if they fall silent from answering [[His saying "i.e., if they fall silent from answering" means they refrained out of cowardice or held back. This is a parable God struck for the truth and its people, and for falsehood and its party, just as He struck the blind and the seeing, and darkness and light, as examples of the two. The likeness of the truth and its people is water which He sends down from the sky, so that the valleys of men flow with it, they are given life by it, and it benefits them in various kinds of benefit; and it is like the metal ore from which they profit [[His words "and like the metal ore from which they profit" — in al-Sihah, "al-filz" (fulz, with a kasra and a shadda on the zay) is what the bellows expel from the substances of the earth that are melted; then let it be verified. Perhaps it is what the bellows leave behind... etc. (ʿAyn)]] in forging ornaments from it and making various vessels and tools; and even if there were only iron, in which there is great might, it would suffice, and that this remains in the earth, enduring with an apparent permanence, while water is retained in its uses. Its traces remain in springs, wells and fields, and in the fruits that grow by it, which are stored and hoarded; likewise jewels remain for long periods. The likeness of falsehood, in its swift vanishing and imminent passing away and its stripping of benefit, is the foam of the torrent that is cast off, and the foam of the metal that floats on top when it is melted. If you ask: why were the valleys made indefinite? I say: because rain does not fall except in alternation among the lands, so some valleys of the earth flow and others do not. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words "according to its measure" (bi-qadarihā)? I say: according to its measure which God knows to be beneficial to those upon whom it rains, and not harmful. Do you not see His words "But as for that which benefits people" — since He struck the rain as a likeness of the truth, it had to be rain purely for benefit, free of harm, and not like some rains and torrents that sweep everything away [[His words "al-suyul al-jawahif" — in al-Sihah, "sayl jahhaf" (with a damma) means a torrent that uproots everything and carries it off. (ʿAyn)]]. If you ask: what is the purpose of His words "seeking ornament or goods"? I say: the purpose in it is like the purpose in "according to its measure," for He combined water and metal in benefit in His words "But as for that which benefits people," since the meaning is: "But as for what benefits them of water and metal," and He mentioned the aspect of benefit from what is kindled upon in the fire and melted, namely ornament and goods. His words "And from that which they kindle upon the fire, seeking ornament or goods" are a comprehensive expression for the kinds of metal, together with showing magnificence in mentioning it in a manner of disdain, as is the habit of kings, like what came concerning the baked brick: "Kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay" (Qur'an 28:38). And "from" (min) is for the beginning of the end: that is, from it arises foam like the foam of water. Or it is partitive, meaning some of it becomes swelling foam, raised and inflated, rising upon the torrent, that is, cast off. "The pot boiled over with its foam" (jaffa'a al-qidr), and "the torrent foamed up and swept along" (ajfa'a al-sayl wa-ajfal). In the reading of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj: "jufalan" (as a plural/ verbal noun). It is related from Abu Hatim: he should not be read with Ru'ba's reading, because he used to eat mice. And it was read: "yuqidun" (with ya'): that is, "what people kindle."

For those who responded (to their Lord), the lām is connected to yaḍribu (He sets forth): that is, thus God sets forth the parables for the believers who responded, and for the disbelievers who did not respond; that is, these are the two parables of the two groups. And al-ḥusnā is an attribute of the verbal noun of istajābū, meaning: they responded with the good response. His statement "Those who have what is in the earth entirely, and the like of it with it" begins a discussion about what is prepared for those who did not respond. It was also said: the speech is complete at His statement "Thus God sets forth the parables," and what follows is a new, independent statement. Al-ḥusnā is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is "for those who responded," and the meaning is: for them is the good reward, which is Paradise. "And those who did not respond" is the subject whose predicate is "law" (if) together with what is in its scope. "The evil reckoning" means the strict scrutiny of it. It is reported from al-Nakha'i that it means a man is called to account for all his sins, and none of them is forgiven.

The interrogative hamza of denial entered upon the fa' in His saying, "Is then he who knows..." (afa-man ya'lamu), to deny that any doubt could arise after the parable that was struck, to the effect that the state of one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, and so responds, is far removed from the state of the ignorant one who has not gained insight and so does not respond. It is like the great distance between the scum and the water, and between the dross and the pure gold (al-ibriz). "Only those of understanding (ulu al-albab) take heed" (innama yatadhakkaru ulu al-albab), that is, those who act according to the dictates of their intellects, so they reflect and gain insight.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 13, verse 20–24:

Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah (alladhina yufuna bi-ahd Allah) is the subject (mubtada'). And as for them, theirs is the good final abode ('uqba al-dar) is its predicate (khabar), like His saying: "And those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation, upon them is the curse" (13:25). It is permissible for it to be an attribute (sifa) of "those of understanding" (ulu al-albab), but the first is more preferable (awjah).

The covenant of Allah ('ahd Allah) is what they bound upon themselves of testifying to His lordship, as in: "And He took witness from them against themselves, saying: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes'" (7:172). "And they do not break the pact" (wa la yanqudna al-mithaq): they do not break any binding agreement they have pledged upon themselves and accepted, namely faith in Allah and other covenants between them and Allah and between them and the servants (al-'ibad). This is a generalization after a specification, "what Allah has commanded to be joined" (ma amara Allah bihi an yusal), of the ties of kinship and relationships. It includes joining the kinship of the Messenger of Allah and the kinship of the believers, which is established by means of faith: "The believers are only brothers" (49:10), through kindness to them according to one's capacity, supporting them, defending them, showing compassion to them, advising them, abandoning division between oneself and them, spreading the greeting of peace among them, visiting their sick, and attending their funerals. Among this is observing the rights of companions, servants, neighbours, and travelling companions, and everyone connected to one by some cause, even the cat and the hen.

It is related from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad that a group entered upon him in Makkah, and he said: "From where are you?" They said: "From the people of Khurasan." He said: "Fear Allah and be wherever you wish. Know that if a servant were to perform every kind of good, and he had a hen and mistreated it, he would not be among the doers of good." "And they fear their Lord" (wa yakhshawna rabbahum), meaning they fear all of His threat; "and they dread" (wa yakhafuna) especially "the evil of the reckoning" (su' al-hisab), so they take account of themselves before they are called to account. "And they are patient" (sabaru): this is unrestricted regarding what one endures of calamities in lives and property and the hardships of obligations, "seeking the Face of Allah" (ibtigha' wajh Allah), not so that it may be said: "How patient and how steadfast he is in misfortunes, how dignified he is at the time of earthquakes!", nor lest he be blamed for impatience and lest enemies rejoice at him, as in the saying:

"And I display to the scorners my fortitude, / that I do not yield to the vicissitudes of time."

And when death sinks its claws in, / you will find every amulet useless.

And display of fortitude to the scorners, I show them / that I do not bow or submit to the turns of fate.

These lines are by Abu Dhu'ayb Khuwaylid ibn Khalid al-Makhzumi, lamenting his sons. It is related that Mu'awiya fell ill, and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, visited him. He said: "Apply kohl to me and dress me in my turban," displaying strength, and recited to him the second verse, and al-Hasan suddenly answered him with the first. He likened death (al-maniyya) to a beast of prey by way of metaphor (al-makniyya). "Insháb al-azfar" (sinking of claws) is an imagining (takhyil). "Mana lahu": he decreed for him. "Al-maniyya": death, because it is decreed.

"Al-insháb": piercing and hanging. "Alfayt": I found, every amulet that does not benefit, which is what is hung on children for fear of jinn and envy. "Tajalladi": your patience and steadfastness, the subject (mubtada'). "Arihim": its predicate, meaning I show them that I do not weaken, submit, or grow feeble because of the vicissitudes of time, i.e., its sudden calamities that come from where I do not perceive.

Nor is it because there is no benefit in anxiety, nor any way of returning what is lost, as in the saying:

"I have neither wailed nor been agitated, / nor will my weeping return a spark."

Beauty is not a garment; / know this, even if you wear a cloak.

Indeed beauty consists of mines / and noble qualities that bequeath glory.

They prepared for calamities a coat of mail / and a swift, long-striding steed.

A nimble, strong one, and a sword with grooves / that cleaves helmets and bodies.

How many a righteous brother of mine / I laid in his grave with my own hands.

I have neither wailed nor been agitated, / nor will my weeping return a spark.

These are by 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib. He says: beauty is not fine clothing. "Fa'lam" is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD), and the address is to an unspecified person: it is not so, even if you dress it and the cloak (burd), a full garment worn over the body. Beauty is praiseworthy qualities that bring honour to their possessors. "Al-hadthan": the disagreeable turns of time. "Al-sabigha": the coat of mail, and he had a coat of gold. "Al-'addaa'": the horse of much running. "Al-'alandaa" (with fatha): the thick, strong, swift one. "Shay' 'alind": hard; "i'landa al-ba'ir": the camel became strong. "Al-nahd": large and tall. "Al-shatb" (with damma): the grooves of a sword. "Al-abdan": short coats of mail; when it cuts through the helmet and the body, though both are of iron, it cuts other things all the more.

He praised himself for courage, then for patience, saying: many of my brothers I placed in their graves with my own hands, yet I did not grieve at all, neither little nor much; "fa-" here is redundant. "Al-hala'": intense distress. In the hadith: "Of the worst of what a servant is given: a miserly greed and a cowardice that tears out the heart," meaning he panics in it as if his heart is torn out. "Tazanda fulan": he was at a loss for an answer and became angry. "Al-mizannad": a proverbial term for a thing. It is said of the insignificant: "a spark in a patched cloak," so "al-zand" is an insignificant thing. It is also narrated as "Zaydan" with ya', meaning Zayd ibn al-Khattab, brother of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who was his friend in the pre-Islamic period. It is also narrated: "Will my weeping return?" meaning: I did not grieve, knowing that it would not benefit.

Every action has aspects in which it is performed, so the believer must intend from among them that by which it is good in the sight of Allah; otherwise he does not deserve reward for it, and the act is like one that has no effect. "Mimma razaqnahum" (from what We have provided for them): from what is lawful, because the unlawful is not provision (rizq).

[Note: the sentence "because the unlawful is not provision" is the position of the Mu'tazila. As for Ahl al-Sunna, it is provision just like the lawful. (Gh.)]
and it is not attributed to Allah

[Commentary: Mahmud said: "The meaning of 'from what We have provided them' is from the lawful, because the unlawful is not provision and is not attributed to Allah Most High." Ahmad said: The truth is that there is no provider except Allah: "Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm" (51:58), just as there is no creator except Allah: "Is there any creator other than Allah?" (35:3). When reason and revelation together require that there is no provider except Allah, what argument then remains for the Qadari who claims that most servants provide for themselves, because most of what they take is unlawful, and yet he remains determined upon his corrupt belief, which neither the scriptural nor the rational admonitions restrain nor deter him? "Then in what statement after Allah and His signs will they believe?" (45:6).]

"Secretly and openly" (sirran wa 'alaniyatan): this includes voluntary acts, since they are better in secret, and obligatory acts, because it is obligatory to make them public to remove suspicion. "And they repel evil with good" (wa yadra'una bi-l-hasanati al-sayyi'ah): they ward it off. From Ibn 'Abbas: they repel with good speech whatever ill others direct at them. From al-Hasan: when they are deprived they give, when they are wronged they pardon, and when they are cut off they join. From Ibn Kaysan: when they sin they repent. It is also said: when they see wrongdoing they command its change. "The good final abode" ('uqba al-dar): the outcome of this world, which is Paradise, because it is what Allah intended to be the outcome of the world and the destination of its people.

[Commentary: Mahmud said: "The meaning is the outcome of the world and the destination of its people..." Ahmad said: The unrestricted term "the outcome" has repeatedly appeared, such as: "And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the final abode" (13:42), and "the outcome is for the righteous" (7:128). In all such cases the meaning is the good outcome and happiness. Al-Zamakhshari infers from the repeated occurrence of the unrestricted term "outcome," meaning the good outcome, that this is what Allah intended, and it is therefore the origin; the other outcome, not being intended but incidental and contrary to the intended origin, should not be expressed except with a restriction that makes it understood, as in "and the outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire." All of this from al-Zamakhshari is a clinging to attributing to Allah a will for what did not occur and a volition for what did not happen, in contradiction to what Allah has made the tongues of the bearers of the Shari'a utter: what Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur. There is nothing in the unrestricted use of this term that indicates it is the origin with respect to will. His act is the origin with respect to command. We say: whatever leads to a praiseworthy outcome is commanded, and whatever leads to a bad outcome is forbidden; therefore the good outcome is the origin. And Allah is the Granter of success.]

"Gardens of Eden" (jannatu 'adn) is a substitute (badal) for "the good final abode." It is read "fa-ni'ma" with fatha on the nun.

The original is ni'ma. Whoever vocalizes the nun with kasra transfers the kasra of the 'ayn to it; whoever uses fatha has made the 'ayn quiescent without transferring. It is also read "yadkhulunaha" in the passive voice. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "salaha" with damma on the lam, though fatha is more eloquent. He informs that lineages do not benefit when stripped of righteous deeds. "And their fathers" (wa aba'ihim) is the plural of the dual of each one of them, as if it were said: from among their fathers and mothers. "Peace be upon you" (salamun 'alaykum) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the meaning is: saying "peace be upon you," or "submitting." If you ask: with what is His saying "bima sabartum" connected? I say: it is connected to an ellipted element, its estimate being: "This is because of what you endured," meaning this reward is because of your patience, or in exchange for the hardships and toils of patience these delights and blessings. The meaning: if you were fatigued in the world, you have now rested, as in the saying:

"The wild animals graze today in the courtyard of al-Hima, / in place of what I used to see there of fair, plump-bodied beloveds."

He says: I see the wild animals grazing in the courtyard of al-Hima in this time, instead of what I used to see there, the beloveds. "Qad ara" is a narration of a past state, with "qad" for approximation. "Al-awanis" is the plural of "anisa" (a maiden). "Al-badan" is the plural of "badina," i.e., fleshy of body.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he would visit the graves of the martyrs at the end of every year and say: "Peace be upon you for what you endured; how excellent is the final abode." [Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari through the transmission of Suhayl ibn Abi Salih from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ..." and mentioned it, adding: "Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman used to do this."] It is also permissible for it to be connected to "salam," meaning: we greet you and honour you for your patience.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 13, verse 20–24:

Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah (alladhina yufuna bi-ahd Allah) is the subject (mubtada'). And as for them, theirs is the good final abode ('uqba al-dar) is its predicate (khabar), like His saying: "And those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation, upon them is the curse" (13:25). It is permissible for it to be an attribute (sifa) of "those of understanding" (ulu al-albab), but the first is more preferable (awjah).

The covenant of Allah ('ahd Allah) is what they bound upon themselves of testifying to His lordship, as in: "And He took witness from them against themselves, saying: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes'" (7:172). "And they do not break the pact" (wa la yanqudna al-mithaq): they do not break any binding agreement they have pledged upon themselves and accepted, namely faith in Allah and other covenants between them and Allah and between them and the servants (al-'ibad). This is a generalization after a specification, "what Allah has commanded to be joined" (ma amara Allah bihi an yusal), of the ties of kinship and relationships. It includes joining the kinship of the Messenger of Allah and the kinship of the believers, which is established by means of faith: "The believers are only brothers" (49:10), through kindness to them according to one's capacity, supporting them, defending them, showing compassion to them, advising them, abandoning division between oneself and them, spreading the greeting of peace among them, visiting their sick, and attending their funerals. Among this is observing the rights of companions, servants, neighbours, and travelling companions, and everyone connected to one by some cause, even the cat and the hen.

It is related from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad that a group entered upon him in Makkah, and he said: "From where are you?" They said: "From the people of Khurasan." He said: "Fear Allah and be wherever you wish. Know that if a servant were to perform every kind of good, and he had a hen and mistreated it, he would not be among the doers of good." "And they fear their Lord" (wa yakhshawna rabbahum), meaning they fear all of His threat; "and they dread" (wa yakhafuna) especially "the evil of the reckoning" (su' al-hisab), so they take account of themselves before they are called to account. "And they are patient" (sabaru): this is unrestricted regarding what one endures of calamities in lives and property and the hardships of obligations, "seeking the Face of Allah" (ibtigha' wajh Allah), not so that it may be said: "How patient and how steadfast he is in misfortunes, how dignified he is at the time of earthquakes!", nor lest he be blamed for impatience and lest enemies rejoice at him, as in the saying:

"And I display to the scorners my fortitude, / that I do not yield to the vicissitudes of time."

And when death sinks its claws in, / you will find every amulet useless.

And display of fortitude to the scorners, I show them / that I do not bow or submit to the turns of fate.

These lines are by Abu Dhu'ayb Khuwaylid ibn Khalid al-Makhzumi, lamenting his sons. It is related that Mu'awiya fell ill, and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, visited him. He said: "Apply kohl to me and dress me in my turban," displaying strength, and recited to him the second verse, and al-Hasan suddenly answered him with the first. "Tajalladi": your patience and steadfastness, the subject (mubtada'). "Arihim": its predicate, meaning I show them that I do not weaken, submit, or grow feeble because of the vicissitudes of time, i.e., its sudden calamities that come from where I do not perceive.

Nor is it because there is no benefit in anxiety, nor any way of returning what is lost, as in the saying:

"I have neither wailed nor been agitated, / nor will my weeping return a spark."

Beauty is not a garment; / know this, even if you wear a cloak.

Indeed beauty consists of mines / and noble qualities that bequeath glory.

They prepared for calamities a coat of mail / and a swift, long-striding steed.

A nimble, strong one, and a sword with grooves / that cleaves helmets and bodies.

How many a righteous brother of mine / I laid in his grave with my own hands.

I have neither wailed nor been agitated, / nor will my weeping return a spark.

These are by 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib. He says: beauty is not fine clothing. "Fa'lam" is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD), and the address is to an unspecified person: it is not so, even if you dress it and the cloak (burd), a full garment worn over the body. Beauty is praiseworthy qualities that bring honour to their possessors. "Al-hadthan": the disagreeable turns of time. "Al-sabigha": the coat of mail, and he had a coat of gold. "Al-'addaa'": the horse of much running. "Al-'alandaa" (with fatha): the thick, strong, swift one. "Shay' 'alind": hard; "i'landa al-ba'ir": the camel became strong. "Al-nahd": large and tall. He praised himself for courage, then for patience, saying: many of my brothers I placed in their graves with my own hands, yet I did not grieve at all, neither little nor much; "fa-" here is redundant. "Tazanda fulan": he was at a loss for an answer and became angry. "Al-mizannad": a proverbial term for a thing. It is also narrated as "Zaydan" with ya', meaning Zayd ibn al-Khattab, brother of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who was his friend in the pre-Islamic period. **Question:** How does their statement, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" (﴿لَوْلا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ آيَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِ﴾), correspond with God's words, "Say: Indeed God leads astray whom He wills" (﴿قُلْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُضِلُّ مَنْ يَشاءُ﴾)?

**Answer:** This statement comes as an expression of wonder at their words. The clear and abundant signs that were given to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were not given to any prophet before him, and the Qur'an alone is sufficient as a sign, one beyond every other sign. When they deny these signs, do not regard them, and treat it as though no sign had ever been sent down to him, this becomes a matter for wonder and disapproval. It is as if they were told: how great is your obstinacy, and how firm is your determination in your disbelief! God leads astray those among those with your attitude who have such determination and such stubbornness in disbelief, so there is no way for them to be guided, even if every sign were sent down. ﴿وَيَهْدِي إِلَيْهِ مَنْ يُنِيبُ﴾ "and He guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance," that is, whoever is of a different attitude from yours. *Anāba* means he turned toward the truth. Its real meaning is that he entered into a state of goodness. ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ "those who believe" is a substitute for *man anāba* (whoever turns back). ﴿وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُمْ بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ "and their hearts find rest in the remembrance of God" means: in the remembrance of His mercy and forgiveness, after the anxiety and agitation caused by fear of Him, like His words ﴿ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ إِلى ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ "then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of God." Or it means their hearts find rest in remembering His proofs, which indicate His oneness. Or it means they find rest in the Qur'an, because it is a clear miracle that calms hearts and establishes certainty within them. ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ "those who believe" is the subject (*mubtada’*), and ﴿طُوبى لَهُمْ﴾ "blessed (ṭūbā) for them" is its predicate. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute for "the hearts," with an omitted modifier, meaning: the hearts of those who believe find rest. *Ṭūbā* is a verbal noun from *ṭāba*, like *bushrā* and *zulfā*. The meaning of "ṭūbā laka" is: you have attained goodness and pleasantness. Its place in the sentence is either accusative or nominative, as in your saying: *ṭayyiban laka*, *ṭayyibun laka*, *salāman laka*, and *salāmun laka*. The reading of ﴿وَحُسْنُ مَآبٍ﴾ "and a good final return" in the nominative and the accusative indicates these two positions. The *lām* in ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ is for clarification, like it is in *suqyā laka*. The *wāw* in *ṭūbā* is changed from a *yā’* because of the *ḍamma* before it, like *muwqin* and *mūsir*. And Makūza al-A‘rābī read *ṭayyibī lahum*, with the *ṭā’* vowelled with a *kasra* so that the *yā’* remains sound, as it is said *bīḍ* and *ma‘īsha*.

Thus We have sent you [as a messenger] in the same manner as that sending: We have sent you with a sending that has a rank and excellence above the other sendings. Then He explained how He sent him, saying: ﴿in a community before which other communities have passed away﴾, meaning: We have sent you to a community that many communities preceded, so it is the last of the communities, and you are the Seal of the Prophets (khatam al-anbiya'). ﴿That you may recite to them that which We have revealed to you﴾, meaning: that you may read to them the great Book which We have revealed to you. ﴿And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾: the condition of these people is that they disbelieve in al-Rahman, the One of abundant mercy whose mercy encompasses everything, and whatever blessing is upon them comes from Him. So they disbelieved in His favour by [rejecting] the sending of one like you to them and the sending down upon them of this inimitable Qur'an, which confirms all the [previous] Books. ﴿Say: He is my Lord﴾, the One who is exalted above partners; ﴿there is no god but He; upon Him I have relied﴾ in my being supported against you; ﴿and to Him is my return﴾, so that He may reward me for my patience and my striving against you.

﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set moving, or the earth split open, or the dead made to speak...﴾ Its answer is omitted, as when you say to your servant, "If only I had risen up to you," and leave out the answer. The meaning is: if a Qur'an existed by which the mountains were set moving from their places and shaken from their resting places, or the earth was cut through until it split apart and broke into pieces, or the dead were addressed by it so that they heard and replied, then this Qur'an would be the ultimate in admonition and the final word in warning and intimidation. This is like His saying, ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of God﴾. This supports what I have explained of His saying, ﴿that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you﴾, namely the intention to exalt what Allah revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of the Qur'an.

It has also been said: the meaning is, if a Qur'an had the effect of moving the mountains, cutting the earth, and speaking to the dead and waking them, they would still not have believed in it nor paid heed to it. This is like His saying, ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels...﴾ the verse.

It has also been said: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Set your Qur'an to move the mountains away from Mecca so that it becomes spacious for us, and we may make gardens and estates in it, as the mountains were made subject to Dawud (peace be upon him). If you are a prophet as you claim, then you are no less honoured before God than Dawud. Make the wind subject to us by it, so that we may ride it and trade to Syria and return the same day, for crossing the great distance has been hard for us, as the wind was made subject to Sulayman (peace be upon him). Or raise for us by it two or three of our forefathers who have died, among them Qusayy ibn Kilab." [[I have not found it in this wording. Ibn Rabi'a related from Abu Usama, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, who said: The Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you are a prophet as you claim, then separate the two mountains of Mecca (I think they are these two), a distance of four or five days, so that we may sow and graze in it, and raise for us our forefathers from the dead so that they may speak to us and inform us that you are a prophet, or carry us to Syria, or to Yemen, or to al-Hira, so that we may go and return in a single night as you claim you did." So Allah the Exalted revealed, ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related through 'Atiyya ibn Abi Sa'id, who said: They said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "If the mountains of Mecca were moved for us until it becomes spacious, so that we may plough in it, or the earth were cut for us as Sulayman used to cut the wind for his people."

Abu Ya'la related from a hadith of al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, who said: "When the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cried out, 'O family of Quraysh!' and Quraysh came to him. He warned them and admonished them. They said: 'You claim that you are a prophet, and that Sulayman had the wind and the mountains made subject to him, and that Musa had the sea made subject to him, and that 'Isa used to revive the dead. So call upon God to move these mountains away from us, and to make the earth burst forth for us with rivers so that we may make it into ploughlands and sow and eat; or call upon God to revive our dead so that we may speak with them and they with us; or call upon God to turn this rock beside you into gold so that we may carve from it and be enriched.' He said: While we were around him, the revelation came down to him. When it passed from him, he said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, He has given you what you asked, and had I willed it, it would have been so. But He informed me that if He gives you that and you then disbelieve, He will punish you.' Then this was revealed."

The meaning of "the cutting of the earth" according to this is cutting it by travel and crossing it.

Al-Farra' said: the phrase is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: ﴿and they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set moving﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interruption. This is not far from correct.

It has also been said: ﴿or the earth was cut through﴾ means it was split and made into rivers and springs.

﴿Rather, the command belongs entirely to Allah﴾ has two meanings. The first: rather, Allah has power over everything, and He is capable of the signs they proposed, but His knowledge that displaying them would be corrupting restrains Him. The second: rather, it is for Allah to compel them to faith, and He is capable of compulsion, except that He founded the matter of obligation upon choice. This is supported by His saying, ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind?﴾ meaning the will of compulsion and coercion. [[His saying "that, if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind, meaning the will of compulsion" is the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) and not of Ahl al-Sunna (the people of the Sunna). (ʿ)]]

The meaning of "have not despaired" (a-falam yay'as) is: have not known. It has been said that this is the dialect of a people of al-Nakha'. It has also been said that "despair" was used in the sense of knowledge because it includes that meaning, since one who despairs of a thing knows that it will not happen, just as "hope" is used in the sense of "fear," and "forgetting" in the sense of "abandoning," because of this inclusion. Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi said:

"I say to them in the ravine when they make me their prisoner: Did you not know (lam tay'asu) that I am the son of the horseman Zahdam?"

[[The explanation of this witness has passed in the first part, page 261; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector)]]

Evidence for this is that 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions and Successors read it as "have not become clear" (afalam yatabayyan), which is an explanation of "have not despaired." It has also been said that the scribe wrote it while drowsy, with the teeth of the letters level. But such things and their like cannot be ascribed to the Book of Allah, to which falsehood does not come from before it or behind it. How could such a thing remain hidden and stay fixed between the covers of the Imam (the standard codex)? It was passed among those eminent, cautious guardians of the religion of Allah, who watched over it, and who were not heedless of its great and subtle points, especially the canon to which reference is made and the foundation upon which the structure rests. By God, this is a slander with no doubt about it.

It is permissible for "that if He willed" (an law yasha') to be connected to "they believed," so that the meaning is: Have not those disbelievers who believed despaired, that if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind, and He would have guided them, ﴿that a calamity will continue to strike them for what they have done﴾ of their disbelief and evil deeds? A calamity (qari'a) is a disaster that strikes them with what Allah brings upon them at all times of the various afflictions and misfortunes in their persons, their children, and their wealth, ﴿or it will settle close to their homes﴾, so that they are frightened and agitated and its sparks fly out to them and its harms reach them, ﴿until the promise of Allah comes﴾, which is their death or the Resurrection.

It has also been said: the disbelievers of Mecca will continue to be struck by a calamity for what they did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by way of enmity and denial, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept on sending out expeditions [[I say: this is found in the Maghazi of Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi, and in the Tabaqat of Ibn Sa'd, in a number of expeditions, among them the expedition of Zayd ibn Haritha to intercept the caravan of Quraysh, and the expedition of al-Hurr ibn Sa'd ibn Bakr, and others.]] which raided around Mecca and seized from them and took some of their livestock. Or, O Muhammad, you will alight with your army close to their dwellings, as happened at al-Hudaybiyya, until the promise of Allah comes, which is the conquest of Mecca, and Allah had promised him that.

Al-Imla' (respite): granting delay, and leaving someone for a span of time in ease and security, like a beast that is left to graze at its pasture. This is a threat to them, and a response to their demand for signs from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), mocking him, and a consolation for him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 13, verses 33–34:

﴿Is then He who stands watch over every soul, for what it has earned,﴾ [this is] an argument against them concerning their associating [others] with Allah. That is: Is Allah, who stands watch over every soul, whether righteous or wicked, for what it has earned, knowing its good and its evil and reckoning out a recompense for each, like one who is not so? It is also permissible to supply what would be the predicate of the subject, and to join to it "and they have made...". Its paraphrase: "Is he who has this attribute [left unacknowledged as one God], while they have made for Him," and He is Allah, who alone deserves worship, ﴿partners.﴾ Say: ﴿Name them.﴾ That is: since you have made partners for Him, name them, tell who they are, and inform Him of their names. Then He said: ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know on the earth...﴾ with "am" (or) being the disjunctive "am" (rather), as when you say to a man, "Tell me who Zayd is, or is he too insignificant to be known?" and its meaning is: "Rather, do you inform Him of partners..." [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: rather, do you inform Him of partners... etc." Ahmad says: The reality of this negation is that they are not partners, and that Allah does not know them as such, because they are not such, even though they have established essences which Allah knows; yet they are created and made to be lordship-subjects, not worshipped gods. But the coming of the negation in this patterned, recited manner is wondrous, and our eloquence and skill cannot grasp it. Had the speech come in its original form, without being adorned by this wondrous variation, it would have been: "They have made for Allah partners, yet they are not partners," and it would not have been placed in this position which the recitation required.]] ﴿of what He does not know in the earth, or of an outward saying?﴾ If He does not know them, it is known that they are not something that knowledge could attach to; and what is meant is the negation that there be partners for Him. Similar to this: ﴿Say: Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth? Or [is it] an outward saying?﴾ Rather, do you call them partners by an outward saying, without there being any reality to it, like His saying ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ and ﴿You worship besides Him only names which you have named﴾. This argument and its wondrous methods, through which it came, is a crier announcing against itself with a fluent, piercing tongue, that it is not the speech of human beings, for whoever knows and is fair with himself. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators. [[He returned to his speech. He said: "This conclusion and its wondrous methods through which it came..." etc. Ahmad says: This conclusion is a true word by which he intended falsehood, for in it he alludes to the createdness of the Qur'an, so be alert to it. How quickly the reader of this section passes over it with his tongue and heart and admires it while heedless of what lies beneath it, were it not for this warning and awakening. And Allah knows best.]]

It was recited ﴿Tunabbi'unahu﴾ with lightening. ﴿Their scheming﴾: their plotting against Islam through their associationism. ﴿And they were barred﴾: it was recited with the three vowel-markings. And Ibn Abi Ishaq recited it with tanwin: ﴿wa ṣaddin﴾.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾: whom Allah forsakes, knowing that he will not be guided, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾: there is no one who can guide him.

﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾: this is what befalls them of killing, captivity, and all other trials. It befalls them only as a punishment for their disbelief, and for this reason it is called a punishment.

﴿And for them from Allah there is no protector﴾: they have no one to guard them from His punishment. Or: they have no one from His side to shield them from His mercy.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 13, verse 35:

"The parable of the Garden" (mathal al-jannah): its description, which is in the strangeness of the parable (ghara'ibat al-mathal). Its subject (mubtada') is in the nominative, and the predicate is omitted according to the view of Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian), meaning: "In what We have related to you is the parable of the Garden."

Someone else said: the predicate is ﴿tajri min tahtiha al-anhar﴾ ("beneath which rivers flow"), just as you say: "Zayd's description is dark-complexioned" (sifatu Zayd asmar).

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "the parable of the Garden: beneath which rivers flow," with the qualified noun omitted, as a representation of what is hidden from us by means of what we witness.

And Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "amthal al-jannah" (the parables of the Garden), in the plural, meaning: its descriptions. ﴿Its fruit is everlasting﴾, like His saying: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾, ﴿and its shade is everlasting﴾, which is not abrogated (la yunsakh), as shade is abrogated in this world by the sun.

And those to whom We gave the Book, meaning those Jews who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Kaʿb and their companions, and those Christians who embraced Islam, who were eighty men: forty from Najran, thirty-two from the land of Abyssinia, and eight from the people of Yemen — these rejoice in what has been sent down to you. And among the factions (al-ahzab) — meaning among their factions, who are their disbelievers who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in enmity, such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib, the bishops of Najran, and their partisans — are those who deny part of it. This is because they did not deny the narratives and some of the rulings and meanings, which are established in their books and unaltered; rather, they denied what is the description of Islam and the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and other things that they had distorted and altered from the laws. 

If you say: How is His saying, ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah﴾, connected to what precedes it?

I say: It is a response to the deniers, and its meaning is: Say, "I have only been commanded, in what has been sent down to me, to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him." So your denial of it is a denial of the worship of Allah and His oneness; so consider what you deny, while you claim the obligation to worship Allah and that none should be associated with Him. ﴿Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is common between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him.﴾ Nafiʿ, in the transmission of Abu Khulayd, read "wa-la ushrika" with a raised vowel (ḍamma), as a new sentence, as if he said: "And I do not associate anything with Him." It is also permissible that it occupy the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in the sense: "I have been commanded to worship Allah without associating anything with Him." ﴿To Him I call⦆ — specifically; I call to none other than Him. ﴿And to Him is my return﴾ — not to any other; and you say the same, so there is no sense in your denial.

And thus We have sent it down: like that sending down, We have sent it down, enjoined in it the worship of God and His unity, the summoning to Him and to His religion, and the warning of the abode of recompense, as a judgment in Arabic (ḥukman ʿarabiyyan), an Arabic wisdom translated into the tongue of the Arabs. Its accusative case (inṣiba) is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

The polytheists used to call the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to matters they would agree with him on, among them that he pray towards their qibla after God had turned him away from it. So it was said to him: "If you follow their desires in a religion that is nothing but whims and doubts, after knowledge has been established with you by proofs and decisive arguments, then God will forsake you so that no helper will help you, and He will destroy you so that no protector will shield you from Him." This is of the mode of stirring up and provoking, and of urging the hearers to steadfastness in the religion and firmness in it, and that whoever holds fast to the proof should not slip when doubt arises. Otherwise, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was of such firmness of resolve as to be beyond any such concern.

They used to find fault with him for marrying and having children, just as they used to say: "What is wrong with this Messenger, that he eats food?" They would also demand signs from him and deny abrogation (naskh). So it was said: the messengers before him were also human beings like him, having wives and offspring. It was not for them to bring signs of their own choosing, nor do they bring what is demanded of them, for the sacred laws (shara'i') are benefits that differ according to circumstances and times. So for every time there is a ruling that is prescribed for the servants, i.e., it is imposed upon them according to what their welfare requires. "Allah effaces what He wills" (﴿يَمْحُوا اللَّهُ مَا يَشَاءُ﴾): He abrogates (yansakh) what He sees fit to abrogate, and establishes in its place what He sees the benefit in establishing, or leaves it un-abrogated. It was also said: He effaces from the register of the recording angels (diwan al-hafazah) that which is neither a good deed nor an evil deed, because they are commanded to record every word and deed. "And He establishes" (﴿وَيُثْبِتُ﴾) what else He wills. It was also said: He effaces the disbelief of those who repent and their sins through repentance, and establishes in their place their faith and obedience. It was also said: He effaces some created beings and establishes others among humans, the rest of the animals, plants, and trees, and their attributes and conditions. Discourse on things of this kind has a wide scope. "And with Him is the Mother of the Book" (﴿وَعِنْدَهُ أُمُّ الْكِتَابِ﴾): the origin of every book, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), since every existing thing is written in it. It has also been read as "wa-yuthbitu" (with the verb in the form in which it is read).
